I know these words were written by my hand, 
some centuries past before thee, Vivian, 
did trap me in a tomb of amber stone.
I know within them hides a glimpse of morrows
one day proven true. My prophecies
are legend. Oracle and sage, the mystic 
mage, Merlin's verse the voice of Delphi.

I know as well for I foresaw its coming
how you trapped me in a jail cell staved 
with tree-root bars. Thou'st needed sunshine free 
of mentor's shadow. Hence I let thee cage
me, mind and body, 'til thee found thy footing
free to walk amongst the trees alone.
Alas, I do not know, nor can I fathom
why thee let me leave my prison cave
bereft of future sight. I read my words
once written with full grasp of deeds
unfolding under moons to come, yet am
a fool before their meaning now. I ask,
dear Vivian, what are thy plans for me?

Thine mentor past and lover still, a trusting 
friend unto the Otherworld beyond.

This verse I wrote four centuries past and had
forgotten every word. 'Til Morgan Fey 
unrolled the scroll and asked me what would follow.
For Arthur's bones now lack his skull and Mordred's 
ghost has turned into a crown thief, stalking 
tombstone hollows. Damned I'd be, were I
to know, my forsooth inklings dried and withered.
The Fey Queen Morgan would not hear my plight. 
She'd known me enigmatic, every word 
a riddle, every phrase a coaxing spell.
We too had once been lovers for a century,
maybe, two. Once learning all I'd had 
to teach, she sprouted wings, away she flew.
And now though I had carefully explained
how Vivian had locked me up and freed 
me leaving mind and soul intact, without 
my power to oracle, nor recall futures seen.

Fey Morgan would not hear of it. She thinks
me old and vain. "While Reverie is dying
Merlin laughs and has his game, 'til demon 
mischief's course is run and all our joys 
unsung." Dear Vivian return to me, I cannot
help without my power of prophecy.

My prophecie when read without my soothing 
sight, give pause to ponder whether weed 
and mead were not at work when put to quill.
Alas the Sandman, Lord of Sleep, I came 
to meet in seeking answers to my blindness.
"Merlin mage, you've wandered far astray.
The only remedy for those who wish 
to see the world that is to be, is planted
deep within your fabled family tree."
And then he proffered me a hero's quest.
"Embrace the Raven's Watch old friend as wizard,
sage and leader. Free our lands of witch's 
minions and your vision shall return."

And so my Vivian off I go to fight
against these foreign demons, well aware 
that my own father born of hellish blood
might run amongst their ilk and fiendish kind.
If this quest should lead to where you keep
my powers locked, I do no longer know.
This journey is a first for me to witness
only that which stands before me in
the now. And so to serendipity 
I vow to take this path where'er it leads.
Your erstwhile wizard sage of Raven's Watch

Again 'tis I who wrote that cryptic verse
some centuries ago. And only now 
is meaning met. Cassandra comes to mind.
In Troy no hero, friend or foe, would heed 
the warning in her words of future doom.
In Reverie my curse is surely worse.
For every word I utter, whether jest
or greetings lightly made is turned
to omen or portentous proof of something
horrid yet to come. Though I protest
and I confess my farsight in me's lacking,
the warriors of the watch are drawn to fear
my reputation as a sorcerer and seer.

For in this hour where witches roam and Nightmares
write anew our fabled tales. I say 
"hello" and off they go headlong into 
battle. I say "goodnight, what starry night"
and sleepless hours await them hatching plans.
I find myself running hither to the fray
a-casting spells to save the day my careless 
words had set so rapidly afoot.
And so my Vivian, I beg for mercy
not for me but those who need truesight.

I dreamt a dream last night, a songe sent by
my devil father speaking with his guile.
He helped me see quite woefully that you
were not the sorceress who'd opened up 
my cage, nor laid the curse to steal the powers
gifted by my spawner. A wailful witch 
named Baba Yaga was she alone to blame. 
"Woe on her, her doom is nigh," according
to my father. Omen spoken, words 
in demon tongue, a prophecy from hell.

Blast this witch of icy climes from o'er 
the Volga vales. I take the fight to Baba!
Her nightmare minions hail from nowhere known
on earth, nor hell, nor Otherworldly realm.
My fellow Raven keepers are too human 
to avail. In fact I've grown too fond of them 
to let them risk their lives in battle with this 
cauldron wielding witch from sleepless hell.
Since every word I speak to them they turn
to prophecy, I've told them I must fight
this fight alone, "'Tis written in the stars."
And so my love farewell to thee, should Baba
Yaga triumph, task to lock this witch 
away and save what's left of Reverie.

Sweet Vivian I have returned a victor
o'er the witch. Our Baba Yaga fought
with savage fury, equal to my spells.
I would have died had not the Watch
appeared in greater numbers than her minions
could repel. She finally fell to druid 
magic, mixed with snow-queen ice, and dragon
fire, a piper's song, a mermaid's chant,
and wolfen warrior's thrashings. Flax-haired maiden 
boy in tow, with Romeo and lovely 
Juliet. Geppetto backed Carmilla as
Aladdin with Wukong closed out our ranks.

My prophecy of single battle, I 
against the witch, they'd thrown aside and leapt
to fray, their superstitions swept aside. 
'twas then I saw what makes a man or woman
brave. To face one's death, a certainty,
defying even fate for greater good.
If prophecy has any worth it cannot
be in champion's song. For future sight 
it sheds no light, but steals the hero's heart.
I must ponder this predicament
until I've learned the lesson meant for me.

At last I now can see just why you locked
your mentor fast in stone. Our fleshly commerce
set aside, our harps, our singing through the night.
There were no future choices made beyond 
the verse your lover voiced in parchment and 
on stone. How ever could you learn from follies
of your own device, if bye and bye 
the words I'd woven traced your every step.

I pen this final missive, dear, written 
without malice. Hopeful how your heart
will read it, for my future sight has went
and gone. I've come to love these days of question: 
mornings bear a sentiment of hope, 'til night
comes all too quickly, sleep a promise of
another day. Finally I have cast 
aside my demon gifts, more truly now 
a human son I've finally become.
Would you, my Vivian, return to love 
a man without a vision for the future? 
Nothing more have I to give, all powers 
you have mastered, all my secrets you've 
revealed. There's nothing left in me but love 
for thee, my harp and legendary wit.

Since I was a little boy, I have always craved the cheering of the crowd. Never have I felt more alive than when navigating in song over a chorus of instruments. My flute would pierce high above the brass and drums, etching emotions on the hearts and minds of bewildered spectators. I called the crowds that gathered my precious flock of songbirds. They called me their maestro.\n\nI often wonder if the pride I felt in such melodious moments was not the cause of the curse that now afflicts me. Perhaps some jealous sorcerer took offense at my popularity, or some wicked wanderer sought glee from my demise. I will one day learn the truth. I have no one left to hear the songs from my youth, and ample time to ponder my predicament.

The curse crept upon me as I slept. A great monstrous dark form appeared to me in a dream, laughing as it cast a spell, proclaiming that the only ears my songs would henceforth please would be those of rats, mice and shrews. 

The next morning when I woke, I was wholeheartedly relieved to learn that this frightful vision had been nothing more than a nightmare. I took out my pipe to play in a nearby plaza and found to my horror that it would only sound songs of sorrow, salted in a key of chaos, peppered on a scale of doom.

My public could not bear to listen to me, putting hand to ear and feet to ground. And sure enough, as the Nightmare had forewarned, my only admirers from that day forward were vile, villainous vermin. The fall from hallowed hall to stinking sewer was a tragedy that took me completely by surprise.

Soon hunger nearly claimed my body, for no town or assembly was client for haunting tunes. I knew no trade other than music, and music, no matter how beautiful or ugly, was little sustenance to a tired body.

I was playing near an oak tree used for hangings, where few people dared to come, when a gentle witch named Baba Yaga took pity on my soul. A host of vermin sat around me, bemused by my playing, the only creatures my songs still beguiled.

Baba Yaga asked why I did not offer my uncomely talent as a service, to rid towns of their rats. The idea was novel, and I was desperate for a meal, so I went to a little town named Hamelin, and asked if they would pay for me to rid them of their mice. They agreed. So I played, and from that day my reputation was made anew. 

I, the Pied Piper of Hamelin, would never again fear for want of food. My pockets now sang with the music of clanking coin. Bodily empowered, I took up a quest to determine who had cast this curse upon me, swearing solemnly to send them to an early grave.

Reverie has many towns, and all of them have rats. As I rid the villages and hamlets of their infestations, four-footed pariah following me away from their drains and sewers, my name grew more famous than it had been as a musician of the classics. 

Though I now had a means of livelihood, I did not consider chasing mice a proper profession, for it meant I walked alone. My mood grew dim as my loneliness grew longer. Even Baba Yaga, in due course, no longer paid me visits. I began to fear I might surely lose my mind. It was one early evening, in my darkest hour of that dark day, that I heard the clanking sound of a shield approach and the snorting sound of a baby dragon. 

I was approached by a captain of the Ravenswatch, its eldest guardian in fact, the old warrior Beowulf, he himself cursedly hounded by a foundling drake. He offered me a place amongst their proud number, if I would swear to hunt Nightmares and chase them from our lands. As desperate for company as I had once been for food, I accepted the offer.

I fought like a devil, playing songs like never before, training my little vermin to do my bidding in this war against the denizens of the dark. The Ravenswatch united many a brave soul under a single purpose – to defeat the Nightmares invading Reverie and banish them from our world.

The tinkerer Geppetto made me flutes like none I had ever played, and Beowulf taught me stratagems to counter enemies on higher ground. Scarlet, Melusine, Aladdin and many more joined me on missions to rid our lands of plague and scorn. 

It was on one fateful night that I crossed paths with a familiar shadow, that of the very witch who I had once counted as my one and only friend. Baba Yaga was giving orders to a trio of Nightmares, as if it were her the commander of their wretched campaign of terror. Was this kind witch our enemy? Was Baba Yaga the sorceress that had cursed my songs? 

That very night, the witch became the focus of my vengeance.

I should have known that Baba Yaga was some evil shrew masked in witchy garb. My music did not scare her, nor did it bend her malicious mind to obey my will. She was somehow immune to all my charms. Convinced that the witch had caused my pipe to play afoul, I set out to kill her, and would not rest until she had died.

On a night without a moon, I cornered Baba Yaga in her den. All my vermin lent me courage, and all my hatred gave me strength. We fought like two demons, hell bent and bloody-eyed, neither giving quarter. Never had I played so well; each note struck home like lightning. And as dawn drew near, the shrew, she finally fell. My rats reared up to shred her into oblivion. 

Then in her eyes I saw a glimmer of the woman who had once shown me kindness. To my surprise, I let her go. She scurried off into the night. I kept this mercy to myself, for I knew that something else was behind our curses, and Baba Yaga was yet another victim. My quest for vengeance had only just begun.

I have come to understand as I play my cursed pipe that this talent is a blessing. No other musician, for I still consider myself a minstrel, knows songs capable of taming the vermin and making them useful in a fight.

I am respected as a warden of Reverie, a guardian of the Ravenswatch. I no longer crave the cheering of the crowd, nor the clapping of king and princess. I prefer to know they all sleep well at night as I chase Nightmares from their dreams. The congratulations of my fellow wardens largely suffice to give me comfort through the night. 

This curse of mine is a gift, and I no longer seek to lose it. A new quest occupies my thoughts, and that is to discover what power truly controls these monsters of the dark and has made our woeful witch serve their true master. When all people and heroes of Reverie are free of this bewildering blight, only then shall I seek a way for me to play songs of joy and laughter once more.

To understand my story, you've got to hear it from the beginning. I loved my gran. Sure, we argued a lot. She was always yelling at me for not wearing dresses and getting my clothes dirty. She didn’t like me learning to hunt and shoot. Thought it wasn’t “ladylike”.
 
I’d blow up at her and would go out to the woods to get some air. Always loved the woods. Something about being around all those trees calmed me. 

That is, until that last time. We had a big blow-up. A major one. I stormed out. Went to be with the trees. 

After I’d calmed down a little, I felt bad about what I’d said to Gran. Started picking flowers to say sorry. Then that damn wolf showed up.

I could tell something was wrong with it. I fought it off, but not before it got its teeth into my arm. Bandaged it as best I could. Hurt like hell. Felt like there was fire in my veins. I raced home to warn Gran about the wolf. 

When I burst through the door, she looked up from her knitting in a panic. She grabbed the '22 stashed behind her chair and pointed it at me. 

I tried to tell her to stop, but the only sound I could make was a strangled howl. I tried to grab the gun from her hands so we could talk, but she pulled the trigger. I smelled gunpowder and blood. Everything after that is a blur. 

When I came to my senses, there was blood everywhere. Gran had been attacked by some wild beast. That damn wolf, I thought! As I got up to go after it, I saw I was covered in blood, too. I felt nauseous. Something was wrong.
 
I caught a glimpse of myself in the mirror by the door and saw with horror that I was the wolf!

The trees couldn't calm my nerves. I found a hole and curled up inside. Maybe it was a nightmare. I'd wake up in the morning and it'd all be over. 

Feet crashing through the underbrush. Voices shouting. Gran's neighbors hunting the wolf that had attacked her. I almost got up to help them, until I realized it was me they were after. Their fear smelled sharp. Enticing. Better stay hidden.
 
When the sun rose, I felt a prickling sensation that turned into a searing heat. Like my skin was turning itself inside out. I looked down and saw that my claws had turned into hands.

Even though I looked normal, I knew I was a monster. I couldn't go home. Too dangerous. I decided to stick to the woods. Keep away from people. Try not to let the beast get the better of me. 

By day, I traveled Reverie in search of a cure. I haunted fairs and markets, taverns and schoolyards. Listening for any mention of some magic that could rid me of the beast.

At night, I hunted.

With every Nightmare I killed, the beast inside me grew. Sometimes the thrill of the hunt was too strong. The wolf took over. I'd wake up covered in blood, thrumming with excitement.

That's how I was when I met Gramps for the first time. I mean Beowulf. He's a grump, but I like him. Reminds me of Gran. Anyway, when he found me, I was all banged up from a brawl with one of those tentacle things. He wanted to help, but I wouldn't let him. Tried to chase him off. Thing is, he didn't run. He wasn't scared of me or my beast. He's got a beast of his own.

He told me I had skill, but that I needed training if I wanted to become a warrior. When he said that, I felt seen for the first time. He wasn't going to coddle me or dress me up in skirts and try to turn me into something I'm not. He gets me.

We hunted together after that. I joined him in the Ravenswatch to kill Nightmares and learn from a master. I became a better hunter. 

But the beast grew stronger, too.

With each transformation, I was more aware of the beast's thoughts. What was once a whisper became a howl. Even when dawn came again and I was myself again, the beast was there, too.

My anger and hatred fed it. It was starting to take over. Even Gramps noticed. "If you're not careful, you're going to lose yourself to the beast," he warned.

The trees didn't help anymore. Piper's melodies riled up the beast instead of calming it down. I spent hours meditating, trying to "close the doors of my mind to the beast". To keep it at bay.

Whenever I opened my eyes, it was there. Ready to swallow me whole.

I heard a rumor that Baba Yaga might be able to help me. I clung to that hope with all my might. If I could find her, I would be cured.

When I finally found Baba Yaga, I was exhausted. Fighting the monsters without and the beast within had worn me down.

But the Witch didn't have the cure I'd been promised. Instead, she revealed she was the source of the nightmares that plagued Reverie.

I got so mad. Furious. Tears of anger welled up in my eyes. I'd been tricked, just like a child. But I wasn't a little girl anymore... My anger filled me with a burning rage. Then it hit me: the anger is me. It's only a curse if I allow it to be one. I'm in control. The choice is mine.

I'd found my own cure for my affliction, even though it wasn't what I'd hoped for.

I let go completely and unleashed the beast within. We fought for Gran, for my old self, for all the victims of those damn nightmares.

Together, the beast and I defeated Baba Yaga for good.

When it was over, I realized that despite my changed form, I was still myself. Not a beast, not a girl. I'm both. 

I'm more.

I may never go back to being the girl I once was, but at last I'm the huntress I was meant to be. I'll continue to fight for Reverie so that everyone can be free!

Dear Romeo, 

Oh Romeo, 'tis thee
who writes these lines with thine own hand.

Ridiculous! I hear thee say. And so 
Thoust speaketh every morn these many moons
since Juliet and thou feigned death and won.

'Tis true your poison ruse was met with great
success. Alas, the price was steep. Thou'st kept
thy wit, but lost come morn its mental purchase.

Heed this early hour to ponder why 
thy written words are nightly lost to mem'ry 
whence thou'st fall to dream, dawn scars attesting
now, that yesterday thy sword was surely 
drawn, thy scratches healed before the dawn.

Be off, now kiss thy Juliet, her heart 
has never faltered, sacred vows she's never 
altered. Daily she remembers all 
since Baba Yaga's curse had last 
transpired. since tragic death you both beguiled. 

Thy Romeo Montagues of Memory Lost

Dear Romeo, again I write to me,

Thee readily shall noteth soon with fright 
how old and tired this letter has become. 
For thou hast read it o'er a thousand times.
Its weathered state bears testament to countless
Frowns, frustrations toll, awrit upon
Thine aging brow, and Juliet's fair face.
So strange a curse to live and then forget.
So strangely blessed revived by Juliet
But as this never ending day grows darker
Thou hast come to doubt, this gift is bent
For if you die your lover dies as well.
So dictates Baba's wicked healing spell.

To blame a witch for all that has befallen
Us, tolls clearer than a morning bell
But truth be known, our present strife is not
the fault of Yaga. Father and our family
Feud is what put turtle doves to flight
And turned our dreams to sleepless frightful nights.
So I implore thee future shadow of 
myself, encourage Juliet with flow'r 
and warming words. She is no more to blame 
than midnight moth aflitting to the flame.

Thine Romeo of Montagues of Family Fought

Dear Romeo, bold Romeo lend ear,
 
At last we've read enough to know these letters
Are from thee. And so 'tis time to speak
about this flock of ravens, brash unkindness,
Juliet and thee have opt'd to join.
We wear the emblem of the Ravenswatch.
These warriors know thy name and worth in battle
Tested by their sides in lines hardheld
against vile hordes invading Reverie. 
So now we quell with quill these mem'ries fled.

The warrior braying fiercely with a dragon 
pup in tow we call sir Beowulf.
And he is often found acourting siren
Melusine although the babe fast in
her belly is not his. Important is 
this detail lest you rend their fragile hoax.
Doth not forget Geppetto who we knew
when we were boy. His toys are now quite deadly,
Keep to mind the nightmares slew his child.
The wizard's name I have forgot, the boy
who sits atop a beast is friend not foe.
The flax-haired maiden soft and sweet is far
more deadly than first gaze would wrongly tell.

Thy Romeo of Heralded Ravenswatch

Dear Romeo, sad Romeo, shed tears,

A melancholy lurks amidst the glee
a fleeting felon peeking through that smile
our Juliet pretends joyful pity free.
And if perchance thou seest clear beyond
the laughter, past pure love's embrace. Know this,
though we are still a child in mind, and she
a princess grown, for sake of love we must
endure. A child to raise was once a hope
we'd fashioned in our dreams of futures shared.
But now I am that boy and she the elder 
sister of a farce the fates begat.

Unworthy of her mindful patience, dull
where she doth shine. A toddler wielding well
his sabre whilst she learneth twice combined.
If tears of sorrow fill thine eyes dry fast
for Juliet must never fears suspect.
Thou hast the day from dawn 'til sleep requires
its restful due, to chase the child and capt
the man she needs thee quickly to become.
The blessing turns to curse whence we forget
that happiness comes never sans its cost.

Thine Romeo of Drying Eyes

Dear Romeo, brave Romeo the bold,

This day thou'st had a vision, how to free
thy Juliet from Charon's chained enchantment
whence thee die so wouldst thy maiden perish.
Death! The caster must endure, for death's
own spell to die, the curse's curser must depart.
Thou art still clever though thy mind is young.
Thou knowst that wither Baba Yaga's spell
has been undone, thy life might forfeit, failing
magic's hold to earthly realms below.
This must be done for Juliet deserves
a life unfettered by thy cursed coil.
The witch, well she must die. Today would be
most fitting for tomorrow never comes.

And now these final words I must address
to thee my sweet, sweet, Juliet.
Forgive me my untelling of our forlorn
paradise. Thou dost deserve a better
end than tied to miscued blasted strife.
If Baba's witchly final breath undoes
my life anon. Then know I leave this stage
with no regret for I have loved. And I've
been loved. And love my soul has wed.

Romeo Montagues of Rightful Quest

Dear Romeo of Witchly Battle Wrought,

The plan was simple, carefully thought, to slay
a witch and make her not, and so we charged
two Lancelots entwined in deathly dance
we fought, to down the nightmare sorceress.
Mad Baba Yaga fought with rage from flying 
cauldron, boiling bile and spitting flames.
With each and every step we took the witch
had counter, Juliet went down to knee.
Thou jumped and jabbed within the secret second
thine own lady had prepared. A trap 
of Capulet device, her plan, your hand.

Within that fateful glimpse of triumph, thou 
didst shatter all resolve to fell the cursed
Architect of thine calamity. 
Forsooth the witch's ghastly plans must end,
Alas, thy life must carry on so long 
as Juliet draws breath. She draws upon
thy youthful hope to fire her guns on sight.
And thou reliest upon her wit to carry 
Thee 'til night, unto the morning light.
The witch's life we spared, her monsters on
the run. Our deadly dance has just begun.

Thy Romeo wed Capulet of Battle Won

Oh Romeo, true Romeo, at last,

Embrace the joy this danger-filled today prepares
For though you will forget the details, bonds
of friendship in the Ravenswatch remain.
It's seen within these warriors' gazes, trust
is not a prize unearned, but given only
After proof of loyalty is learnt.
For thou hast found eventful purpose side
by side with Juliet. The life you two 
have forged from sorrow, tempered nightly in
the waters of the Styx, is chance for thee
to love delightful fired by newness, wonder
ever kindling kisses stolen from the grave.

'Tis also chance for her to grow and ponder, 
brightly thinking, smarter grinning, ever 
fonder of the man thou hast become. 
There is no shame for two sound souls to walk 
as one. Each day its share of novelty.
Each night its share of unexpected love. 
I lift a glass to future dawns when children
born from blessed compromise, will call
to me their father mindful I've forgotten
all their names but not the love I store.

Mine Romeo of Lifted Heart

In the days before the Darkness covered the land, my kingdom was a very different place. The sun shone warm, the hills were verdant, and the fields were fertile. Our people were peaceful and joyous, with few causes for concern and many causes for celebration.

I acceded to the throne after the death of my parents, King Kai and Queen Gerda. From the moment the mantle of rulership was clasped around my shoulders, I swore to protect the kingdom from harm just as I would protect my own family. For indeed, following my parents' untimely death, I was left in charge of my infant sister, Lily.

I ruled the kingdom with a fair and gentle hand, the same way I raised Lily, and both flourished. I used my healing powers to keep illness and evil at bay. Our nation prospered under my benevolent stewardship.

In the seventh year of my reign, when the roses were in bloom and the people were preparing to celebrate summertide, disaster struck. A winter storm rose in a single night, bringing with it a blizzard that left a blanket of snow over the land. Nightmares rode in on the wind, torturing those they met and turning their minds to madness.

I opened the palace doors to shelter my citizens from the cold and from the Nightmares' touch. Those within the palace walls survived the cold night. Once the storm passed, I led a party to succor any survivors. 

The destruction was devastating. Nary a trace of vegetation was left: there was only white, as far as the eye could see. More terrible yet, there was no movement in the landscape, save for the Nightmares in search of fresh victims.

The wounded were brought to the palace. I went from one sickbed to the next, providing such healing as I could. It was my duty as Queen to come to the aid of all those in need. After healing the last citizen, as I yearned for respite, my faithful aide whispered urgently: "Come quickly. It's your sister."

Lily's face was contorted, and she raged wildly. When I went to her bedside, Lily shrieked and lacerated me with a blade of ice hidden in her bedclothes. It shattered, and a sharp pain shot through my breast. 

My aides held her writhing form as I laid my hands on her to free her from the Nightmare that possessed her. But this was in vain. The shard of ice that had pierced my heart had corrupted my healing touch.

Instead of healing my dear, sweet Lily, she died, frozen by my own hand.

Even in the darkest of times, a Queen's duty is to her people. I had no time to grieve. The kingdom was in crisis. I summoned my most brilliant counselors and savants to understand whence this evil had come. But not even the wisest of men could tell me how this could have been prevented, nor how to put an end to it.

For indeed, the winter was never-ending. Day after day, the sun rose over the glittering snows that had buried my kingdom. Many began to despair that they would never see a rose in bloom again.

Whispered rumors came to my ears. Dark mutterings in corners. Some thought I was to blame: they spoke of a royal curse. They thought my malediction proof of some dark stain in my family's past that had brought this evil down on our kingdom. 

I could not permit such ill misgivings to fester in the darkness. I gathered my people and made a formal proclamation: I myself would set out to find the source of the evil and put a stop to it, to return our kingdom to its true state. I swore that, as their monarch, I would not rest until I had restored peace and tranquility to our land once again. 

With that, I left my council to rule in my stead, and I set out on my own to right the wrong that had been done to my kingdom, as befits a ruler. Such is the fate that was thrust upon me, and I accepted this heavy burden with dignity.

In my journeys, I encountered the warriors of the Ravenswatch, who also strove to chase the nightmares from our lands. I agreed to join their ranks and fight alongside them, as long as they served my purposes. I aimed to find the source of the darkness and cast it out. If the Ravenswatch could help further my aims, all the better.\n\nHowever, I had not anticipated the band of misfits and eccentrics such an organization would contain. Among the ranks of the Watch I found a few kindred spirits, but most were fools and weaklings who would be of no use to me. Time and again, I found myself carrying the heaviest share of our burden.

When I finally found the source of the darkness, I discovered Baba Yaga was its source. Emboldened by my righteous vengeance, I vanquished my foe and ended her reign of terror. \n\nAs my wrath abated, I looked around and caught a glimpse of myself in a looking glass. With horror, I realized that what I saw was not the triumph of good over evil. What I saw, instead, was one cold-hearted queen standing over the dead, broken body of another. But to what end? To claim her place and reign in her stead? Is that what I had been after all this time?

Vengeance for vengeance's sake is hollow, I realized. Baba Yaga's death would not return my dear Lily to me, nor would the nightmares disappear along with her. Reverie had been changed forever, and we must change with it. I must change with it.

In the Ravenswatch, I had met a host of well-meaning souls united in a common cause. Though I took them for fools, I saw that a great good had come of our struggle: together, we were capable of more than any one of us could do individually. For the first time, I realized that I was not alone.

I returned home and to the surprise of all, I left the kingdom in the capable hands of the council who had ruled in my absence. My last decree as sovereign was to order the borders opened to all those who will stand against the nightmares. If there is to be hope for Reverie's future, it shall come from working together. 

This shall be Lily's legacy.

Who better to tell the story of the fall of Sun Wukong than Sun Wukong himself? I am named Heaven's Equal by immortal demons and eternal queens alike. I mastered the 72 powers of transformation. I escaped the mythical mountain after five hundred years in chains. I know the names of every monkey ever born. I am the Monkey King, the greatest warrior to ever walk the worlds of Reverie.

My brush weaves words as gracefully as my staff wreaks havoc. I am the equal of all poets. This is my tale to tell. This is the magnificent story of the tainting of my crown by jealous, fiendish rivals which led to my great demise, doomed to walk among mortals and their shattered dreams. 

It is said that every great warrior needs a great foe, just as a good carpenter needs good wood. I shall defeat these Nightmares who have kept their names a secret. Just as a clap cannot produce sound with a single hand, neither can a god be slain before the deaths of his rivals.

The dead go, the living stay. So was it written on my palace walls, where I ruled with mirth and marvel. To live is to dance in celebration of all the treasures the heavens have bestowed upon us. In my palace, music filled the air like petals grace the wind, announcing the coming of cherries and plums. The only law I set to enforce was that of constant celebration.

Sorcerers received open invitations, so long as they could dance or sing or amuse us with some trick worthy of my palace. In my zealous generosity, I had forgotten a teaching of my master: "You cannot live near cinnabar without becoming red, nor ink without becoming black." Would I have remembered this, I would not have opened my doors to a sorceress dressed in black and her thousand shadow dancers.

The promise of seeing a thousand shadows dance seemed worthy of my halls, which were so brightly lit that all normal shadows had been chased away by the exuberant lights. The only payment the sorceress asked for was the right to kiss my crown. And so out they poured from her chest to greet my guests. So much blackness from a box was thrilling, until the shades ripped through my entourage, and put an end to our festivities.

As morning light dispersed the darkness from my tarnished halls, and lust of battle fled my veins, I was taken with a pain I had never before felt. My immortal blood dripped from several wounds I had taken in the fight that would not heal. My foes had fled, their dark deed done. My guests were dead or gone.

This mysterious sorceress had cast a curse upon my crown, and now I was mere mortal, vulnerable to death. Sun Wukong could not die here. I must make my story right. What the mouth speaks means nothing; only deeds can be judged.

I wandered Reverie in search of the dark sorceress and her thousand shadow dancers. I met a piper who knew not of the sorceress – but said my description of the shadow dancers reminded him of what he called Nightmares. He proposed that I join the Ravenswatch and fight amongst their wardens, who had vowed to rid the world of these demons. 

I laughed at the man and went on my way. I am Sun Wukong, Heaven's Equal. I do not fight alongside mortals; they would only slow me down. How could mortals be worthy of mention in my spectacular tale?

Days went by, and I could find no trace of the sorceress who had cursed my crown. I came to feel that the shadow dancers feared me and so refused to fight. I then remembered a teaching of my master. "Sit by the river long enough, and the bodies of your enemies will come floating in the current."

After seven eternal minutes of waiting that nearly drove me mad, a beautiful woman came by, her hand spitting ice, freezing the stream so she could cross. I quickly went to her and asked if she were a goddess. She replied in haste: "I am a queen. I have not time for conversation; I am chasing a Nightmare."

I jumped to follow her, despite her forebodings, and for a moment I thought she might turn me to ice. "I am Sun Wukong, Heaven's Equal and the King of all Monkeys. I am on a quest to defeat the thousand shadow dancers of an evil dark sorceress. She has cursed me and made me mortal." The queen stared at me with a glare that could have frozen an ocean before saying words that put a fire into my heart: "You can join me, so long as you can keep up."

I had been made mortal by a treacherous sorceress, but my prowess in battle is the broth of legend's soup. I am cast of the iron reserved for statues at the heavens' gates. Monsters I destroyed. Nightmares I chased. Witchly plans I foiled. Yet still the wardens showed me little respect and would not make me their king.

Tethered by my mortal coil, it proved difficult to outfight my unequals in battle against the monsters. I could pounce like a tiger but no longer jump from mountain top to mountain top. I could run faster than a breeze but no longer outrun the winds. Still, I made certain to be the first warrior to charge our foes in battle, even when the other wardens called for a stupider strategic approach. The fruit does not wait to fall according to the will of the tree, but rushes to the ground with determination, regardless of the bruises it knows it will suffer.

I lunged, tail flying, facing three Nightmares with nothing but my staff. For the first time in my glorious existence, I tasted the sour milk of defeat. Wounded, I fell, with eyes wide open. I could see nothing but stars. I thought I would now visit the halls of death, but it was not my time. My mortal life was saved by Nyss, the Snow Queen, the Sorceress of Ice, and now the Salvation of Heaven's Equal. I would not be alive to write my glorious tale of doom and demise had it not been for that mortal's intervention. My shame was godly, the redness on my face brighter than the sun.

The next day, my tail had lost its bounce, and my head weighed heavy on my shoulders. The skies cried drops of heavy tears, for when a god knows shame, the heavens weep. It was then that I heard the screams of villagers and, without thinking, ran to defend them. I laid low a dozen monsters and a Nightmare that day – and caught a glimpse of the sorceress who had kissed my crown. My foe was Baba Yaga. My vengeance had a name!

After that battle, much to my surprise, the wardens of the Watch began to treat me with measured dignity. The piper boy played a song for me. The old warrior chanted a poem. Nyss, the mortal sorceress, took my godly paw and shook it proudly. She told me that I was a fool, but a brave one, that had saved a dozen souls of Reverie that day. "This time," she added, "you knew you could die."

Like a riddle from my master, Nyss's words gave me pause. Are these humans in their mortal bodies braver than we gods? They fight always knowing that each moment might be their last. Their lives a tiny pebble thrown into a giant ocean, their tiny ripples fighting tide and waves to change the fate of Reverie. I remembered then my master saying something about a butterfly causing a cyclone... or might it have been the sneeze of a dog?

I found Baba Yaga and had her life at my mercy. I ordered her to remove the curse upon my crown, to take back her putrid kiss. She laughed at me and told me she was proud. I, the Monkey King, Heaven's Equal, had defeated her in the body of a mortal. What greater fate was there than that? She would gladly now remove my curse so that I might return to my former life of deathless glory.

I sensed in her words a trap. How could I return to being a god when I had become the greatest of all mortals? Ah, the clever witch. All my great feats of courage would lose their savor if I were to be freed of death and my powers returned. I refused that she undo her dreadful kiss. I would wear a tarnished crown, for under it I had made myself a champion equal to no other, equal not only to the heavens but all the hells as well.

I was now the greatest hero of Reverie. A god made mortal, a warrior worthy of all titles. I, Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, Heaven's Equal, and worthy to be king of Ravenswatch. All that was left was to convince my fellow wardens.
